body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud about sunlight (RI.K.1, SL.K.2).
- Students directly compare two objects, one in the sun and one in the shade, to tell which is warmer (K.MD.A.2), and describe what they felt (SL.K.4).
- Students draw and tell about a structure that makes shade, naming what it is and how it helps (W.K.2, SL.K.5).
- Science focus: sunlight warms the Earth's surface; blocking sunlight makes shade, which is cooler.

MATERIALS
- Two matching dark rocks, blocks or squares of dark paper; a sunny spot and a shady spot outside (or a sunny windowsill and a shelf)
- Building materials for shade: craft sticks, paper, cloth scraps, tape, cardboard, clay
- A small tray of sand or soil and a desk lamp, if it is cloudy all week
- Crayons and paper, or tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read The Warm Sun together. In the morning, put one rock in the sun and one in the shade. Ask: what do you think will happen? Leave them until after lunch.
Day 2: Lesson activity: The Sun Warms Things. Read the text aloud twice; students answer by speaking. Then go outside and touch both rocks from Day 1.
Day 3: Sun or Shade: Which Is Warmer? Students repeat the test with two new matching objects, feel them, and record their comparison. Talk about what was the same (the objects) and what was different (sun or shade).
Day 4: Make Some Shade. Read the sandbox problem aloud. Students draw a shade maker and tell how it works. If you can, build a few with craft materials and test them over the sand tray in the sun or under a lamp.
Day 5: Assessment: Sun and Shade Check. Read the story and each question aloud twice. Students answer by speaking and draw one way to make shade.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: let students hold both objects at once and say "this one" before naming sun or shade. Offer the words warm, warmer, cool, cooler on picture cards.
- Support: offer a starter drawing of the sandbox so students only add the shade maker.
- Stretch: ask students to test whether a bigger shade maker keeps things cooler than a small one, and to tell which material blocked the most sunlight.
- Multilingual learners: act out warm (fanning) and cool (rubbing arms) and point to the sun and the shade while you say the words. Accept answers in the home language first, then build the English sentence together.
- Safety: on hot days check that metal or dark surfaces are not hot enough to hurt before students touch them, and keep the lamp away from hands.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week your child is learning that sunlight makes things warm and that shade keeps things cooler. On a sunny day, try this together: touch a sidewalk or step in the sun, then one in the shade. Which is warmer? Ask your child to tell you why. You can also look for shade makers on a walk: trees, umbrellas, porches and awnings.
title: Teacher guide: Sun and Shade
